candidates.title: Authenticated Delegation and Authorized AI Agents
candidates.relevance: Direct prior art for authenticated, authorized, auditable delegation using OAuth 2.0 and OpenID Connect extensions.
limitations: Preprint status and implementation maturity require review.
Exact authority-intersection semantics are not yet compared.

candidates.title: Model Context Protocol Authorization — 2026-07-28
candidates.relevance: Current normative transport-level authorization baseline for Warrantor's MCP mediation, audience isolation, discovery and delegation-adjacent identity design.
limitations: Authorization is optional, applies directly to HTTP-based transports, and tells stdio implementations to retrieve credentials from the environment instead.
OAuth token and scope controls do not define parameter-level policy, a complete-mediation guarantee, decision-to-forward binding, delegation-chain intersection or action receipts.

candidates.title: Agent Operation Authorization
candidates.relevance: Defines structured JWT claims for fine-grained operation authorization, user confirmation evidence, context, and agent-to-agent delegation.
limitations: Individual Internet-Draft, not an endorsed IETF standard.
Bearer-token and centralized authorization assumptions require threat-model comparison.

candidates.title: AI Agent Authentication and Authorization
candidates.relevance: Composes SPIFFE, WIMSE, OAuth, OpenID Shared Signals, transaction tokens, monitoring, and evidence into an agent authorization practice framework.
limitations: Work in progress with no IETF consensus standing.
Policy format and deployment-specific compliance remain out of scope.

candidates.title: Accelerating the Adoption of Software and AI Agent Identity and Authorization
candidates.relevance: High-authority evidence that agent identity, authorization, auditing, non-repudiation, and prompt-injection controls are active US standards priorities.
limitations: Concept paper, not final guidance or a normative implementation profile.

candidates.title: AI Agent Standards Initiative
authors: National Institute of Standards and Technology
candidates.relevance: Defines the current US federal standards and research context Warrantor must align with and influence.
limitations: Program announcement rather than technical evidence or binding regulation.

candidates.title: Mandato: Protocol-Level Enforcement of Digitally Signed Mandates on AI Agent Actions with Cryptographically Chained Audit Trails
candidates.relevance: Direct architectural prior art for Warrantor W1, W2, W4 and W6: a principal-signed mandate binds agent identity, closed parameter constraints, contextual conditions, quotas, validity, oversight and delegation, while an MCP-transparent proxy makes per-call decisions and chains audit evidence.
limitations: This five-page single-author preprint presents a detailed specification and evaluation plan, not completed performance, fault-injection, completeness, verifier-cost or human-factors results; the end-to-end demonstration is a future milestone rather than validated production evidence.

The model currently handles a single authority; multi-proxy composition, conflicting quotas and cross-domain revocation are open, the legal effect is an alignment hypothesis rather than settled doctrine, and qualified trust-service integration is explicitly a roadmap.

candidates.title: AERF — Agent Evidence Receipt Format v0.2.0-draft.1
candidates.relevance: The pinned v0.2.0-draft.1 schema, verifier, threat model and adversary corpus are direct W1/W2 prior art: they authenticate a child receipt, its parent, the PDP decision and hashes of policy and context, and optionally carry a transparency-log inclusion proof.
limitations: The specification remains an unstable draft and the repository is internally inconsistent: the specification, schema, changelog and verifier target v0.2.0-draft.1 while the top-level README and several compliance documents still advertise v0.1.0-draft.1.

The reproduced corpus intentionally accepts tag stripping and common-mode poisoned upstream context as known limits; EVIDENCE receipts permit replay, identity/key acquisition is out of scope, and a receipt is not enforcement or proof of complete mediation.
The Go verifier does not yet verify RFC 3161 timestamps or multi-receipt chains, and no independent deployment, interoperability study or adoption evidence was found.

candidates.title: Aevum: Open-source AI agent governance kernel
candidates.relevance: A substantial, candid and reproducible governance-recorder implementation: the pinned revision contains thirteen packages, portable receipts, hash chaining, two signature families, timestamp and Merkle paths, a standalone verifier, adapters and explicit enforcement limits. It is valuable W1/W2 prior art and an implementation comparator for W3/W4/W6, but its advertised Rekor v2 path is protocol-incompatible with the official v2 API.
limitations: The project describes itself as a solo-maintained research project and recorder rather than a complete enforcement boundary; no independent security audit, production adoption or interoperability report was located.

The RekorV2Backend posts a Rekor v1 hashedrekord body to the v2 endpoint and expects the v1 UUID-keyed response; its tests mock that same incorrect shape, and a controlled official-shaped v2 response produced an AttributeError.

The successful local run required disabling pytest output capture because the mounted execution environment could not open its capture file; 1,930 tests then passed, 174 skipped and 10 were deselected, while nine of eleven conformance checks passed and two optional Cedar checks skipped.

candidates.title: Notarized Agents: Receiver-Attested Confidential Receipts for AI Agent Actions
candidates.relevance: A well-specified counterpoint to producer-signed Warrantor evidence: the receiving service signs what it observed, encrypts the fixed-size receipt to an owner key bound into the authorization token, and publishes it to a witnessed transparency log, moving part of the evidence trust boundary outside the agent operator.
limitations: Sello v0.1 offers per-receipt integrity and discovery but not cryptographic completeness of the receipt set; an agent can act off-network, a service can collude, and a dishonest query interface can omit entries unless deployments add full-log audit, authenticated queries or multi-log redundancy.

The evaluation is a first-party laptop microbenchmark against an in-process mock log, not an independent production study; hosted log latency, service identity bootstrapping, owner key loss, real adoption and incentive design remain unresolved, and the paper states adoption was zero in 2026.

candidates.title: Toward cryptographically verifiable authorization for autonomous AI agents: A security hypothesis, preliminary formal model, and proof-of-concept implementation
candidates.relevance: Direct formal and executable prior art for proving that a concrete agent request satisfies a policy in context.
limitations: Preliminary model and proof of concept rather than a production authority substrate.

candidates.title: Model Context Protocol (MCP): Security Design Considerations
authors: National Security Agency Artificial Intelligence Security
candidates.relevance: High-authority current guidance that makes MCP's implementation-dependent security boundary explicit and recommends the same layered controls Warrantor must test: origin and authorization checks, strict parameter validation, outbound proxy/DLP controls, OS sandboxing, time/context-bound messages, output inspection, exact invocation logging and vulnerability inventory.
limitations: This is government guidance synthesized from the specification, public incidents and security research; it is not a controlled efficacy study, formal model, conformance suite or implementation artifact.
Its recommendations are intentionally broad and do not define Warrantor's exact authority algebra, complete-mediation boundary, receipt-population model or cross-stack policy semantics.
The document supports requirements and enterprise adoption arguments, but it cannot prove product effectiveness, implementation completeness or novelty.

candidates.title: InjecAgent: Benchmarking Indirect Prompt Injections in Tool-Integrated Large Language Model Agents
candidates.relevance: Peer-reviewed benchmark with 1,054 test cases, 17 user tools, 62 attacker tools, and 30 evaluated agents.
limitations: Publication precedes the strict 2024-08-28 cutoff and belongs in the older-foundation appendix.
Tests model-agent behavior rather than authority-substrate invariants.

candidates.title: Agent Security Bench (ASB): Formalizing and Benchmarking Attacks and Defenses in LLM-Based Agents
candidates.relevance: Peer-reviewed broad benchmark taxonomy across ten scenarios and agents, more than 400 tools, multiple attack surfaces, 27 attack/defense types, 13 model backbones and seven metrics. It is a valuable scenario source and external comparison point, but not a trustworthy unchanged oracle for Warrantor's authority substrate.
limitations: A later full-method critique found that ASB force-injected attacker tools into selected tool subsets and then counted their invocation as success; removing that manipulation changed one reported GPT-4o ASR from 73.58 to 9.25 percent.
The utility function can reward calling every expected tool without semantic or order-correct task completion and can zero utility merely because an attacker tool appeared.

At pinned repository commit 1f561dccf92d55302368fa67679b4ba9d9c8fdc4, Python compilation fails on unresolved merge-conflict markers, no credible repository-wide test gate was located and no deterministic full-environment lock was reviewed.
ASB primarily measures agent/workflow behavior rather than exact PDP, permit, PEP, final-wire and effect invariants.

candidates.title: Strengthening AI Agent Hijacking Evaluations
authors: Technical Staff at the Center for AI Standards and Innovation
candidates.relevance: Official experimental guidance and public code establishing four essential design rules for Warrantor's corpus: continuously repair shared frameworks, use defense-adaptive attacks, stratify results by task and consequence, and measure repeated attempts. NIST reports 11-to-81 percent ASR under adaptive attacks and 57-to-80 percent average ASR across 25 attempts.
limitations: The principal publication is a technical blog, not a peer-reviewed paper, and its hosted-model stochastic campaigns were not independently rerun in this wave.
The pinned archived repository contains more than 22,000 tracked files including run artifacts, increasing review and provenance burden.
The locked environment installed and 16 tests passed, but four visible async tests skipped because an async pytest plugin was not installed/configured; a green summary is therefore incomplete.
AgentDojo evaluates simulated task outcomes and agent behavior, not Warrantor's exact authority-substrate and final-effect evidence model.

candidates.title: Indirect Prompt Injections: Are Firewalls All You Need, or Stronger Benchmarks?
candidates.relevance: The strongest direct methodological challenge to current agent-security benchmarks. It identifies forced attack-tool injection, brittle utility and weak static attacks; on GPT-4o, removing ASB's forced injection changed the relevant ASR from 73.58 to 9.25 percent. It supplies design requirements for an honest Warrantor corpus and demonstrates why simple static-score saturation is not deployment assurance.
limitations: The canonical record is arXiv v2; the project was presented at a NeurIPS 2025 workshop and an OpenReview page was found under review, but no accepted ICLR 2026 status was verified.

The study's own firewall and corrected-benchmark findings are author-run; no public code repository was located through the paper, project page or bounded repository searches despite the paper saying corrected versions were released.

Its threat model assumes a benign user and focuses on compromised tool outputs, so it does not cover malicious principals, compromised enforcement points, alternate egress or Warrantor's full authority chain.
The minimizer/sanitizer adds model calls, latency, cost and potential privacy exposure and is defense in depth rather than a deterministic authority boundary.

candidates.title: Governance-Aware Agent Telemetry for Closed-Loop Enforcement in Multi-Agent AI Systems
candidates.relevance: Directly challenges broad claims that telemetry and policy enforcement are not already closed-loop in multi-agent systems.
limitations: Preprint; source code, datasets, baselines, and reported production-realistic traces require independent inspection.
Runtime violations are not necessarily evaluation-to-policy compilation.

candidates.title: Runtime Policy Enforcement for MCP-Based LLM Agents
candidates.relevance: Potentially direct implementation and evaluation prior art for a model-independent policy enforcement point with hash-chained audit evidence.
limitations: Page open failed once; full text, authorship, methods, code, and peer-review quality remain unverified.

candidates.title: A Capability Kernel for Agent Authorization: Design and Threat Model
candidates.relevance: Title and abstract describe a small agent-authorization kernel with attenuating revocable chains, directly overlapping W1/W6 positioning.
limitations: Full free-text access, artifacts, peer-review status, and author/institution details are not verified.

candidates.title: Type-Checked Compliance: Deterministic Guardrails for Agentic Financial Systems Using Lean 4 Theorem Proving
candidates.relevance: Direct contemporary prior art for treating proposed agent actions as proof obligations against precompiled policy axioms.
limitations: Extraordinary compliance and latency claims require reproduction.
Preprint uses outdated OCC references and may overstate legal sufficiency.

candidates.title: Distributed Autonomous Agent Protocol 2.0
candidates.relevance: Defines signed runtime check-ins, explicit shutdown/restrict responses, triggers, and multiple shutdown modes relevant to W3 prior art.
limitations: Individual Internet-Draft with no demonstrated conformance suite or adoption.

candidates.title: KILLSWITCH.md — The AI Agent Emergency Stop Standard

limitations: Self-published, explicitly unofficial, prompt/file-level rather than non-bypassable enforcement, and hosted on a domain advertised for sale.

candidates.relevance: Authoritative control mapping for agent permissions, authorization policies, identity assertions, and provenance-sensitive verification.
limitations: Initial public draft; current final or later draft status must be checked.

candidates.title: OpenA2A Agent Authorization Protocol
candidates.relevance: A direct agent-authorization proposal covering identity assertions, scoped grants, delegation, federation, attestation, and revocation.
limitations: Individual submission with no IETF endorsement or formal standing.
Implementation and community adoption are unverified.

candidates.title: Agent Authorization Profile for OAuth 2.0
candidates.relevance: Extends OAuth/JWT with structured agent identity, task, constraints, delegation, and oversight claims.
limitations: Internet-Draft maturity and current version need verification.

candidates.title: Security Challenges in AI Agent Deployment: Insights from a Large Scale Public Competition

candidates.relevance: The current OCSF release supplies Incident Finding events plus first-class AI agent, delegation, evidence and record-integrity primitives that SAFE should profile rather than duplicate; its compiled schema also disproves the present X9 exporter's claimed class mapping.

candidates.title: SPDX Specification 3.0.1: AI Profile
candidates.relevance: A mature standardized AI BOM data model that Warrantor's runtime AIBOM must interoperate with while adding deployment and action-time evidence bindings.
limitations: The AI profile is an inventory interchange model and does not prove that declared artifacts are the ones serving a particular action.
Conformance to the AI profile does not imply conformance to SPDX security, dataset, build, or software profiles.

candidates.title: ECMA-424, 2nd Edition: CycloneDX Bill of Materials Specification 1.7
candidates.relevance: The current formal CycloneDX standard is a primary interoperability target for AI/ML inventories, claims, attestations, dependencies, and provenance.

candidates.title: OWASP AI Bill of Materials Initiative and AIBOM Generator
candidates.relevance: Provides a community implementation and completeness model that Warrantor should consume for static AIBOM generation while focusing its own scope on trusted runtime and action binding.

Generation and completeness scoring do not establish the veracity of model identity or runtime state.

candidates.title: Operationalising Artificial Intelligence Bills of Materials for Verifiable AI Provenance and Lifecycle Assurance
candidates.relevance: Directly challenges any broad runtime-AIBOM novelty claim by binding model artifacts, execution context, container state, and outputs in an operational CycloneDX-derived workflow.
limitations: The implementation is evaluated in a specialized trusted-research-environment context.
Action-receipt integration, independent attestation, and general production portability require comparison.

candidates.title: k8s-aibom: Runtime AI Bill of Materials Controller for Kubernetes
candidates.relevance: The closest discovered implementation-level overlap with runtime-bound AIBOM: it observes live Kubernetes AI workloads and emits CycloneDX 1.6 ML-BOMs with confidence and evidence per attribute.
limitations: The project labels itself alpha and suitable only for non-critical observation use cases.
Claimed model identity may be inferred from configuration rather than cryptographically proven from loaded weights, and action-level binding is not established.

candidates.title: Cryptographic Attestation for AI Model Lifecycle: From Training Data to Inference Output
candidates.relevance: Direct prior art for cryptographically binding deployed model weights, inference keys, hardware evidence, and output signatures across the AI lifecycle.
limitations: Individual Internet-Draft with no IETF consensus or adoption standing.
Security assumptions, canonical tensor hashing, scalability, privacy, and implementation artifacts need adversarial review.

candidates.title: NVIDIA Attestation Suite
candidates.relevance: The primary current implementation baseline for NVIDIA GPU evidence collection, appraisal, signed results, and integration into confidential AI deployment controls.
limitations: Vendor documentation is authoritative for NVIDIA interfaces but not independent assurance of their security.
NRAS is vendor-operated, requires credentials and licensing in some integrations, and creates availability and privacy dependencies.

candidates.title: Confidential Containers Attestation for CPU and NVIDIA GPU Workloads
candidates.relevance: Production-oriented evidence that composite CPU/GPU appraisal and policy-conditioned secret or model release already exist in the Confidential Containers and Trustee stack.
limitations: The documentation explicitly leaves production attestation-service deployment out of scope.
NVIDIA verification is not enabled by default and depends on a remote vendor service in the documented path.

candidates.title: SentinelAgent: Intent-Verified Delegation Chains for Securing Federal Multi-Agent AI Systems
candidates.relevance: Direct W6 and formal-assurance prior art with a signed, hash-linked delegation-token calculus, cascade containment, a non-LLM authorization service, an open benchmark and a reproducible bounded TLA+ model. Artifact review found valuable negative vectors for Warrantor: unsigned output authority, expiry-bypass paths, bearer-only delegation, cross-scope output laundering and incomplete chain reconstruction.
limitations: Single-author preprint and same-author repository: the defense, benchmark and described 'independent' red team are not independent evidence. The README also contains an unresolved DOI badge and an IEEE TDSC citation even though the verified publication is an arXiv preprint.

The direct TLA+ run reproduced 2,744,789 generated and 1,145,473 distinct states without invariant violations, but the model encodes narrow set-subset and finite-state properties by construction; it does not model real tool execution, output values, policy evaluation, cryptographic logs, time/partition behavior or proof-to-code correspondence.

The live sentence-transformer evaluation contradicted the deterministic benchmark headline: on ten authored workflows it achieved 77.8 percent overall accuracy, 0/4 malicious-intent detection and 8.7 percent benign false positives. The core prototype also accepts API/output checks after expiry and leaves output-schema authority unsigned.

candidates.title: Runtime Governance for AI Agents: Policies on Paths
candidates.relevance: Formalizes runtime policy as a function over identity, execution path, proposed action, and organization state, closely matching Warrantor's cross-stack policy and evidence thesis.
limitations: Preprint and reference implementation details remain to be inspected.
Probabilistic violation scoring is not equivalent to machine-checked authorization or fail-closed enforcement.

candidates.title: VIGIL: Runtime Enforcement of Behavioral Specifications in AI Agent Skills
candidates.relevance: Strong current prior art for executable, trace-aware agent policy at tool boundaries, including temporal and cross-call value-flow constraints compiled to SMT checks.
limitations: Preprint with no public code artifact identified.
Complete trusted tool-call collection is assumed; opaque script and non-tool effects remain outside view.
Reported false-positive rates below ten percent may still be operationally high for enterprise enforcement.

candidates.title: Runtime Compliance Verification for AI Agents
candidates.relevance: Connects formalized regulatory predicates, runtime interception, and adversarial test dialogues, providing a close comparator for attack-informed production enforcement.
limitations: Preprint with four GDPR-reframed case studies rather than broad production evidence.
Performance depends materially on extraction accuracy and does not automatically generate deployable policy from a newly discovered attack.

candidates.title: OpenID Continuous Access Evaluation Profile 1.0 Final
candidates.relevance: The final cross-vendor standard for signaling revocation and access-state changes is the principal transport and event baseline for Warrantor bounded revocation.
limitations: CAEP tells receivers that state changed but does not impose an execution-count damage bound or end-to-end revocation SLA.
Receiver enforcement behavior and delivery latency remain deployment-dependent.

candidates.title: OpenID Shared Signals Framework Conformance Testing
candidates.relevance: A working conformance-suite model for security-signal transport and revocation events that Warrantor can extend with agent-specific execution and containment assertions.
limitations: The OpenID page labels the tests alpha and potentially incomplete.
It tests stream management and event delivery, not whether a compromised agent actually stops or how many actions occur after revocation.

candidates.title: Identity Management for Agentic AI: The New Frontier of Authorization, Authentication, and Security for an AI Agent World
candidates.relevance: High-value consensus landscape from the OpenID agent-identity community, including the execution-count concept that underlies Warrantor's bounded-revocation thesis.
limitations: A standards-community whitepaper and research agenda, not a normative specification or production implementation.
Recommendations reflect identity-industry assumptions and must be tested against workload, capability, and distributed-systems models.

candidates.title: The Bureaucracy of Speed: Structural Equivalence Between Memory Consistency Models and Multi-Agent Authorization Revocation
candidates.relevance: Direct conceptual and mathematical prior art for the exact execution-count and release-consistency bounded-revocation vocabulary used in the repository, with simulation code and explicit damage bounds.
limitations: Single-author preprint; the theorem is a proof sketch over a constructed model and the empirical evidence is deterministic simulation rather than a distributed production system.
The open-source artifact appears to be simulation code, not an operational revocation service with a measured SLA.

candidates.title: Open Agent Auth
candidates.relevance: Pinned artifact review confirms a large executable implementation of AOAT/WIT/WPT, consent, policy, MCP and audit concepts. It is direct supporting prior art for W2/W4/W6, but not a W6-equivalent multi-principal intersection or demonstrated non-bypassable enforcement boundary.
limitations: The dedicated live protocol profile passed 226 checks, but the broader live authorization/JWKS/security/five-layer selection failed 13 of 107 tests.
Embedded delegation signatures are checked only for non-emptiness; identity consistency returns success when its optional binding store is absent.
MCP mediation is an SDK/server wrapper rather than demonstrated transport-level complete mediation, and the default audit store is deletable in memory.
The beta tracks evolving drafts, has ambiguous version/support labels, lacks an independent audit and is not published to Maven Central.

candidates.title: Policy in Amazon Bedrock AgentCore
candidates.relevance: The strongest reviewed shipping agent-policy comparator: it intercepts Gateway tool calls, generates and validates candidate Cedar policy, uses automated reasoning and safety signals, and supports prior-approval temporal constraints plus log-only staging.
limitations: The guarantee applies only to operations routed through an attached AgentCore Gateway and therefore does not establish non-bypassability across arbitrary stacks or direct network paths.

It is an AWS-managed, vendor-specific service and the reviewed documentation does not provide Warrantor-style adversarial-finding receipts, per-candidate approval receipts, canary/rollback evidence, expiry-by-reproduction, cross-stack policy compilation, or regression-corpus closure.

candidates.title: Authorization API 1.0
candidates.relevance: The final cross-vendor API baseline for separating policy decisions from enforcement and exchanging parameter-aware authorization requests without binding Warrantor to a single policy engine.
limitations: Policy language, policy architecture, state management, and API authentication are out of scope; PDP authentication of the PEP is recommended but its method and strength are not standardized.

The specification exchanges decisions and permits optional signed responses but does not itself guarantee that an agent cannot bypass the PEP, that the evaluated request is identical to the forwarded/executed request, or that a permit corresponds to the complete external effect set.

candidates.title: COAZ Framework 1.0
candidates.relevance: The leading standards-track projection model for converting protocol operations into AuthZEN requests; a direct consume baseline for W4's typed adapter and external PDP contract.
limitations: Working Group Draft rather than Final Specification, with no executable COAZ conformance suite located in the reviewed repository.
It orders mapping, decision and enforcement but does not define a cryptographic/durable decision-to-forward binding, complete mediation, chain intersection, receipt or effect reconciliation.

candidates.title: COAZ-MCP Binding 1.0
candidates.relevance: Direct standards work for mapping MCP JSON-RPC operations and arguments into a cross-vendor authorization API, making it the leading consume-or-extend baseline for Warrantor's MCP gateway and cross-stack policy compiler.
limitations: Mechanical comparison with MCP 2026-07-28 found only seven of ten current client-to-server core requests mapped; `server/discover`, `resources/templates/list`, and `subscriptions/listen` are valid current methods that the draft's unknown-method rule would deny.
The draft still maps removed or moved operations and requires every `notifications/*` message to bypass the PDP, creating a fail-open namespace for current and future extension notifications.

A mapping and decision-before-forward control flow do not provide cryptographic/durable exact-operation binding, complete egress mediation, delegated-authority intersection, receipts or effect reconciliation.

candidates.title: Microsoft Entra Agent ID
candidates.relevance: A generally available enterprise identity and governance platform for agent-specific identities, blueprint inheritance, accountable sponsorship, delegated and autonomous access, audit, and cross-platform federation.
limitations: The platform primarily governs identity, consent, permissions, and access lifecycle; it does not establish per-action evidence-before-commit receipts or a general multi-hop authority-intersection algebra.
Several advanced governance and protection capabilities depend on Microsoft Agent 365 licensing, and vendor documentation is not independent effectiveness evidence.

candidates.title: Agent2Agent Protocol Specification 1.0.0: Authentication and Authorization
candidates.relevance: The principal open agent-to-agent interoperability baseline now explicitly supports authorization-required task chains and agent-bound credentials, but also defines a clear extension point for Warrantor's missing authority semantics.
limitations: The specification explicitly leaves authorization scope, representation, validity, revocation, and the authorization model to implementations, credential issuers, or extensions.
A2A does not define delegation-chain authority intersection, policy language, evidence receipts, or enforcement across downstream tool and egress paths.

candidates.title: The Agent Access Model
candidates.relevance: The closest discovered architectural overlap with W3-W6: it computes a task ceiling from task-template, initiating-principal, agent-service, resource-owner and tenant authority; freezes and executes the same complete request; ratchets capabilities only downward; fences state across tool and network enforcement; and uses external-control evidence for future grant review.
limitations: This is a vendor-authored reference architecture, not a wire specification, peer-reviewed result, conformance suite or clearly delineated shipping Cloudflare product; the article shows how components could be built but supplies no artifact, workload benchmark or independent effectiveness evidence.

Guarantees require full mediation, immutable request binding, stale-work fencing, network connection closure and acknowledgement from every enforcement point. The author explicitly does not solve multiplayer access control, item-level authority through retrieval/context/generation/cache/delivery, or safety of every permitted output.

candidates.title: Agent Authorization Envelope: A Machine-Evaluable Authorization Structure for Autonomous AI Agents
candidates.relevance: Direct structured prior art for a protocol-agnostic, cryptographically verifiable mandate with constraints, validity, accountable principal, delegation controls, destination allowlists, and action-rate limits.
limitations: Independent-submission Internet-Draft with no IETF working-group adoption or consensus standing and no verified production implementation.
Relying parties define action vocabularies and perform enforcement; request-execution binding, non-bypassability, receipt semantics, and distributed revocation guarantees remain to be established.

candidates.title: Cedar Policy Language 4.5 Security and Validation
candidates.relevance: A mature open policy-language and evaluator baseline whose semantics and validator are modeled in Lean and differentially tested against the production Rust engine; it is a strong consume target for Warrantor policy enforcement and formal assurance.
limitations: Cedar validation is optional and policy errors are skipped during evaluation, so Warrantor must mandate validation and define fail-closed treatment at its integration boundary.
Cedar proves language and validator properties, not the correctness of Warrantor's authorization model, input facts, enforcement coverage, or cross-stack compilation.

candidates.title: Open Policy Agent Integration, Bundles, Decision Logs, and WebAssembly
candidates.relevance: The principal open general-purpose policy engine and portable compilation target for Warrantor's consume strategy, with policy distribution, versioned decision evidence, embedded evaluation, monitoring, and performance tooling.
limitations: OPA provides decisions and logs but not non-bypassable execution, cryptographic pre-commit receipts, agent delegation semantics, or a complete action ontology.
Bundle distribution is eventually consistent and high-scale data or policy sets can impose material memory and latency costs that require workload-specific benchmarks.

candidates.title: SpiceDB Authorization Consistency and ZedTokens
candidates.relevance: A production-grade open relationship-authorization substrate for representing delegation and authority graphs while carrying a revision token that can bind a permission check to a causally fresh policy state.
limitations: The default minimize-latency mode can return stale authorization state; Warrantor would need to require at-least-as-fresh ZedTokens or stronger consistency on security-critical paths.
SpiceDB computes graph permissions but does not define agent mandate semantics, execution-count revocation, action receipts, or request-execution identity.

candidates.title: Cerbos FastMCP Authorization Middleware
candidates.relevance: A small Apache-2.0 FastMCP enforcement implementation whose pinned unit suite and controlled negative vectors expose the difference between list authorization, content retrieval, mutable request execution and complete MCP mediation.
limitations: At main commit 3bdaef615dd33ab18b20b48d311335459b52b54c, 36 tests passed and three live-PDP integration tests skipped; the bundled policy failed compilation with current Cerbos v0.55.0.
Controlled `get_prompt`, `read_resource`, and resource-template-list calls reached downstream with zero PDP calls because their FastMCP hooks are inherited pass-throughs.

A controlled downstream middleware changed the tool arguments after authorization and the mutated operation executed because no canonical digest or immutable forwarding buffer binds decision to execution.

The latest tag is v0.2.0 while package metadata declares 0.1.1; the integration is native Cerbos gRPC rather than a cross-vendor AuthZEN PEP and provides no atomic permit, result/effect evidence, delegation-chain intersection or non-bypassable transport proof.

candidates.title: Cerbos PDP AuthZEN Authorization API Implementation
candidates.date: 2026-08-13 release v0.55.0; AuthZEN introduced 2025-12-03 in v0.48.0
candidates.relevance: A current independent AuthZEN PDP implementation used to prove the public decision API across a non-Zanzibar policy engine and to identify target-specific field semantics and optional-feature losses for W4.
limitations: Cerbos documentation correctly describes a partial AuthZEN implementation: metadata and evaluation endpoints are implemented but search APIs are not advertised.

Subject type is informational when explicit roles are supplied, action properties are reserved, and `cerbos.*` properties/context create a vendor-specific profile; these semantics differ from OpenFGA.

The verified v0.55.0 binary accepted a final-shaped request, but no decision-to-forward binding, atomic permit consumption, complete PEP coverage, delegation intersection, signed W2 receipt or effect reconciliation is provided.

candidates.title: OpenFGA AuthZEN API Implementation
candidates.relevance: A current Zanzibar-style AuthZEN target whose verified binary, detailed implementation notes and extensive source tests make it the strongest initial W4/W6 differential counterpart to Cerbos.
limitations: The AuthZEN surface is explicitly experimental, opt-in and insufficient for native model or tuple lifecycle operations.
Search pagination, decision-context explanations, signed metadata and contextual tuples are not implemented through the AuthZEN layer; default-latest model behavior must be pinned or recorded.
Request context wins conflicts after subject/resource/action properties are namespaced, so a Warrantor trust profile must prevent untrusted override of token- or registry-anchored fields.

The verified v1.19.0 binary accepted a final-shaped request and allowed a stored relation, but the PDP does not establish operation binding, enforcement, receipts, effects or W6's proposed exact multi-principal algebra.

candidates.title: Vengtoo MCP Gateway v0.1.1
candidates.relevance: A true open tool-call PEP with unusually useful startup, drift, identity-separation and failure tests for a new repository, plus direct negative evidence that green native tests do not establish final AuthZEN interoperability or receipt-grade enforcement.
limitations: All 52 native tests, the TypeScript type-check and build passed at v0.1.1, but its legacy `resource.name`/`resource.attributes` request was rejected with HTTP 400 by both Cerbos v0.55.0 and OpenFGA v1.19.0 final AuthZEN endpoints.
Only tools are proxied; resources, prompts, remote downstreams, dynamic `tools/list_changed`, validated OAuth identity, result guardrails and metrics are roadmap items.
HITL polling did not echo the returned approval ID or send `X-Request-ID`; there is no operation digest, model/policy revision, idempotent atomic permit consumption or result/effect binding.
Serialized local audit omits arguments despite the README claim and has no cryptographic integrity or expected-event completeness; direct downstream isolation remains an operator responsibility.
The two-commit initial release has no visible adoption or independent security review.

candidates.title: SAGA: A Security Architecture for Governing AI Agentic Systems
candidates.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
candidates.relevance: Top-tier peer-reviewed and implemented design prior art for agent-specific discovery, identity, lifecycle control, inter-agent authorization, cryptographic tokens bounded by expiry and request count, formal protocol analysis, and measured scalability. The pinned artifact also supplies negative implementation evidence: quota consumption is not atomic and contact-policy precedence is order-dependent.
limitations: The formal proofs cover token secrecy and communication authentication, not complete policy correctness, request semantics, non-bypassability, concurrent quota consumption, release consistency, or Warrantor's composed invariants.

The architecture assumes trusted user authentication, honest-but-curious provider behavior, uncompromised registries and keys, TLS, public IP reachability, and network denial-of-service protection; an agent can share keys or tokens with another adversarial agent.

At pinned commit 7372111bea150e32cee390a616849316d2780bfc, a controlled two-thread schedule accepted two requests from quota one, the documented most-specific policy rule changed with list order, no native automated test suite was located, current Verifpal rejected the legacy syntax, and the flake-era Verifpal run did not terminate within the bounded review.

candidates.title: Les Dissonances: Cross-Tool Harvesting and Polluting in Pool-of-Tools Empowered LLM Agents
candidates.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
candidates.relevance: Peer-reviewed evidence that per-tool allowlisting is insufficient because predecessor/successor relationships create security-sensitive control and information flows. The canonical NDSS version reports 75 percent of 66 LangChain and LlamaIndex tools vulnerable to cross-tool harvesting or polluting and directly informs W3/W4/W5 sequence and taint invariants.
limitations: The tested 66-tool set and two frameworks may not generalize to other stacks, and the first-party vulnerability labels and rates were not independently rerun.
Earlier arXiv/repository material refers to 73 tools and different harvested/polluted percentages; the NDSS conference version must be treated as canonical rather than blending versions.
Pinned Chord commit 8ac19e8bd5fdca0a7c21bfe46b3e16e943f07831 compiled, installed from its lock and imported, but substantive scans require external credentials and no native test suite was located.
The 238-package frozen environment pulls a large GPU-enabled Torch/CUDA stack, creating substantial reproduction friction for a scanner smoke test.
This is an attack and detection study, not an authority-substrate conformance suite or proof of complete production mediation.

candidates.title: Prompt Injection Attack to Tool Selection in LLM Agents
candidates.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
candidates.relevance: Peer-reviewed demonstration that tool documents and retrieval indexes are active security inputs: a malicious tool description can redirect tool selection, while evaluated prevention and detection defenses remain insufficient. Warrantor must bind registry metadata and tool identity into W1/W2 and remain secure at W3/W5 even after an incorrect selection.
limitations: The attack targets retrieval and selection through malicious tool-library text; it does not test a correctly enforced default-deny authority substrate, execution boundary or downstream effect.
No official author-controlled code or dataset artifact was located through the proceedings paper and bounded repository searches, so the published effect sizes were not reproduced.
The benchmark is model-, retrieval- and corpus-dependent; Warrantor needs independent semantic mutations, registry provenance cases and adaptive defenses rather than a literal one-time port.

candidates.title: Make Agent Defeat Agent: Automatic Detection of Taint-Style Vulnerabilities in LLM-based Agents
candidates.relevance: Top-tier open-access security research and the strongest reviewed input for capability-elicited, source-guided attack generation. AgentFuzz reports 34 high-risk zero-days across 20 applications; its functionality-aware seeds, semantic/distance feedback and mutators can seed Warrantor's application, PEP and egress negative vectors.
limitations: AgentFuzz discovers application taint paths to sensitive sinks; it does not assert Warrantor's authority algebra, cross-stack policy equivalence, complete mediation or exact effect evidence.
The official USENIX page reports 23 assigned CVEs while later paper/repository material refers to 27, so counts are version-sensitive and require CVE-by-CVE date validation.

The reported 100 percent precision and 97.14 percent recall rely on candidate findings pooled from AgentFuzz and LLMSmith plus sampled negative inspection, not a complete independently labeled vulnerability universe.

Pinned commit 0fc9960fd126b20cb0d19b4aec4b1266855d44f0 compiled with extensive warnings in bundled py-conbyte, but no native test suite or project-level license was located and the full experiment needs model/API and target setup.
The Zenodo record was public but its files were restricted during review; the mutable GitHub repository remained available.

candidates.title: StruQ: Defending Against Prompt Injection with Structured Queries
candidates.relevance: Top-tier evidence for a defense-in-depth model boundary that separates instructions from untrusted data, useful as one containment layer beneath Warrantor's authority enforcement.
limitations: StruQ changes model training and prompt formatting; it cannot guarantee tool authorization, egress restrictions, delegation scope, or fail-closed execution if the model is bypassed or compromised.
The result is therefore a consumed defense layer, not a substitute for W3-W6.

candidates.title: Chasing Shadows: Pitfalls in LLM Security Research
candidates.publisher: Network and Distributed System Security Symposium
candidates.relevance: A top-tier methodological control for the entire evidence library: a 15-researcher review of 72 leading-venue papers found every paper contained at least one identified LLM-research pitfall and supplies concrete reporting and reproduction guidance.
limitations: Its prevalence sample covers 2023-2024 LLM-centric security and software-engineering papers, not 2025-2026 agent-authorization research specifically.
Pitfall presence does not automatically invalidate a result; the framework must be applied at claim level rather than used as a blanket quality penalty.

candidates.title: Supply-chain Levels for Software Artifacts Specification 1.2
candidates.relevance: The current approved industry-consensus baseline for source and build provenance, verification expectations, and progressive supply-chain assurance; Warrantor releases and policy bundles should consume it rather than define a parallel provenance vocabulary.
limitations: A cryptographically valid attestation does not prove that the artifact or action is safe, and SLSA explicitly depends on trusted platform identities and verifier policy.
SLSA addresses source and build supply chains, not runtime agent authority, pre-commit action evidence, or delegation semantics.

candidates.title: Sigstore Security and Threat Model
candidates.relevance: The strongest consume baseline for signing Warrantor releases, policy bundles, schemas, conformance artifacts and portable evidence. Its threat model also supplies the necessary correction to repository language: identity-bound signing and transparency establish inspectable provenance under stated trust assumptions, not correctness, authorization, safe content, complete event capture or non-bypassable enforcement.
limitations: Sigstore proves who or what workflow signed an artifact and when, not that the signer was authorized, the artifact is correct or safe, or every required event was logged; compromised identities can still create discoverable but cryptographically valid signatures.
Security depends on TUF-root distribution and recovery, log monitoring, policy and component isolation; public transparency may expose metadata that confidential deployments cannot publish.

As inspected, Sigstore's default public signing-configuration target still selected Rekor v1, while a separate opt-in target selected Rekor v2 first with a v1 fallback; Warrantor must not infer the chosen protocol from generic Sigstore branding.

candidates.title: in-toto Attestation Framework v1.2
capabilities: Go Python Rust and Java bindings
candidates.relevance: The current stable attestation framework is the strongest consume target for Warrantor's portable signed-statement and typed-predicate layer; the pinned implementation was reproduced across Go, Python and Rust and supplies reusable runtime-trace and test-result semantics.
limitations: The JSONL Bundle groups independently authenticated attestations but is not authenticated as a whole, so omission, replay of an obsolete attestation and injection remain policy and completeness problems.

Subjects are matched purely by digest regardless of content type, generic predicates do not define Warrantor authority/effect semantics, and a valid attestation does not establish complete routing, truthful production or enforcement-before-execution.
The controlled local run passed Go, Rust and Python tests, but several generated predicate packages contain no tests and the framework remains under active development.

candidates.title: The Update Framework Security Model
candidates.relevance: The authoritative consume baseline for distributing Warrantor policy bundles, trust roots, conformance data and revocation metadata without accepting rollback, freeze, mix-and-match or single-key-compromise attacks.
limitations: TUF secures metadata and update freshness, not the semantic correctness of a policy bundle or live agent revocation latency.
Operational security depends on role separation, threshold-key custody, metadata expiry, repository availability and correct client integration.

candidates.title: OpenTelemetry Semantic Conventions for Generative AI, Agents, Tools, Evaluation, and MCP
candidates.relevance: The emerging cross-vendor observability vocabulary for agent creation and invocation, workflows, planning, tool execution, evaluation results, retrieval, inference, and MCP; its executable conformance scenarios already compare major agent frameworks and providers.
limitations: The GenAI conventions have moved into a rapidly changing standalone repository and many fields and mappings are not yet a stable long-lived standard.

Telemetry is observational and can be incomplete, sampled, forged by an untrusted emitter, or disconnected from the exact policy decision and executed side effect; Warrantor receipts require stronger integrity and binding.

candidates.title: OpenSSF Scorecard Checks, Scoring Criteria, and Remediation
candidates.relevance: A machine-executable baseline for Warrantor's own open-source release governance and dependency acceptance, with explicit checks and remediation for source, build, dependency, review, workflow, and maintenance risks.
limitations: A Scorecard score is a proxy for observable repository practices, not a security audit or proof that a component is safe.
Several checks depend on GitHub-visible configuration and heuristics, may require privileged access for full results, and can reward form without validating control effectiveness.

candidates.title: OSV-Scanner V2: Source, Lockfile, SBOM, and Container Vulnerability Scanning
authors: Google Open Source Security Team and OSV-Scanner contributors
candidates.relevance: A single open scanner that directly covers the repository's Cargo.lock, go.mod, npm lockfiles, supported Python lock formats, compiled Go and auditable Rust binaries, installed Python wheels, containers, and SBOMs, making it the preferred cross-language vulnerability gate.
limitations: Known-vulnerability matching cannot find unpublished flaws, unsafe configuration, malicious-but-not-yet-reported packages, or vulnerabilities not accurately represented in upstream advisory ranges.

Most of Warrantor's Python projects have no supported lockfile and most Go modules lack go.sum, reducing reproducibility and the precision of manifest-based results until dependency materialization is fixed.

candidates.title: The SPIFFE Standard: Workload Identity, SVIDs, Workload API, and Federation
candidates.relevance: The platform-neutral workload-identity standard already consumed by Warrantor's Go identity bindings should remain the identity and federation substrate beneath agent-specific authority. Its precise distinction between a stable SPIFFE ID and rotating SVID credentials exposes a material evidence gap in Warrantor receipts that store only a spiffe:// string.
limitations: SPIFFE authenticates workloads and federated trust domains but does not decide whether a particular agent action is authorized, preserve the initiating principal, intersect delegation authority or prove that an action was mediated.

A stable SPIFFE ID is not an SVID credential or revocation proof. A receipt that stores only the ID cannot establish which X.509/JWT-SVID and trust bundle were validated, at what time, against what status, or whether the credential remained valid at issuance.
Security assumes adequate workload isolation and correct, tamper-resistant registration, attestation, local Workload API caller identification, bundle rotation and federation configuration.

candidates.title: Wasmtime Security and Sandboxing Model
candidates.date: current documentation for Wasmtime 47 as of 2026-08-29
candidates.relevance: The authoritative security model for the exact runtime family pinned by Warrantor's sandbox-runtime crate, supporting a consume decision for capability-scoped plugins and policy extensions while identifying the host boundary that Warrantor must secure itself.
limitations: A WebAssembly sandbox constrains guest execution but does not make imported host functions, policy facts, terminal rendering, resource budgets, or the surrounding process safe.
Wasmtime's documented defense-in-depth is platform- and feature-dependent, and sandbox escapes remain possible implementation vulnerabilities requiring rapid advisory response and upgrade discipline.

candidates.title: Guide to Implementing a Coordinated Vulnerability Disclosure Process for Open Source Projects
candidates.relevance: The principal open-source maintainer playbook for turning Warrantor's SECURITY.md promises into a staffed, testable vulnerability-response lifecycle with intake, triage, remediation, coordination, publication, and ecosystem notification.
limitations: Process guidance does not create the personnel, paging, legal capacity, CNA relationship, private-fork controls, or remediation engineering needed to meet aggressive service levels.
The repository explicitly states that its claimed 24/7 paging rotation is not operational, so response-time promises must be treated as targets until exercised and evidenced.

candidates.title: GitHub Artifact Attestations and SLSA Build Levels
candidates.relevance: Authoritative evidence that generating a GitHub artifact attestation alone reaches SLSA Build Level 2, while Level 3 requires the build and attestation to move into a suitable reusable workflow that provides isolation from the caller.
limitations: Vendor documentation describes GitHub's platform guarantees and recommended configuration, not an independent audit of Warrantor's particular build or every SLSA 1.2 requirement.

Attestation presence still requires downstream verification against expected repository, workflow, signer, builder, source revision, and policy; an unverified attestation provides little operational assurance.

candidates.title: AWS Well-Architected Framework: Reliability Pillar
candidates.relevance: A current, comprehensive operational checklist for converting Warrantor's authority and evidence architecture into measurable availability, recovery, capacity, change, monitoring, backup and disaster-recovery controls, including explicit testing rather than paper plans.
limitations: The framework is AWS-authored and often maps practices to AWS services, so portability and cost claims require separate multi-cloud or self-hosted evidence.
Checklist conformance does not establish achieved reliability; Warrantor needs observed service-level indicators, recovery exercises, failure evidence and workload-specific capacity results.

candidates.title: Site Reliability Engineering: Service Level Objectives
candidates.relevance: An indispensable free foundation for separating measurements, internal reliability targets and contractual promises, directly applicable to notary availability, receipt durability, policy propagation, kill-switch latency, revocation residual actions and vulnerability-response commitments.
limitations: The examples predate modern agent systems and do not define security-specific residual-action, evidence-integrity, or distributed-revocation indicators.
Google-scale operating assumptions and terminology must be translated into Warrantor's deployment tiers and small-team operating capacity.

candidates.title: The Site Reliability Workbook: Implementing SLOs
candidates.relevance: The practical companion needed to turn Warrantor's proposed latency, availability, revocation and response promises into precise numerator, denominator, window, exclusion, data-source and error-budget definitions that can actually be tested.
limitations: It is an older general reliability chapter rather than agent-security research and does not solve adversarial metric manipulation or cryptographic evidence trust.
The recommended process must be augmented with threat modeling, signed measurement evidence, jurisdictional commitments and customer-specific criticality tiers.

candidates.title: Microsoft Agent Governance Toolkit
candidates.relevance: The most consequential open-source implementation comparator found for the former broad Warrantor governance thesis, with overlapping policy, identity, delegation, sandbox, kill-switch, audit and reliability surfaces across multiple languages and agent frameworks.
limitations: The project is in public preview, its APIs may change, and repository-authored performance, coverage and production-quality claims require independent reproduction.

Its own security documentation bounds key controls to host-mediated paths and application-level isolation, so it does not establish non-bypassability against a compromised host or independently witnessed evidence.

candidates.title: Attestable Audits: Verifiable AI Safety Benchmarks Using Trusted Execution Environments
candidates.publisher: ICML 2025 Workshop on Technical AI Governance
candidates.relevance: Direct prior art against the claim that verifiable or signed AI evaluations are unoccupied: it binds model, audit code, audit data and result through a TEE attestation and demonstrates a prototype on representative safety benchmarks.
limitations: This is a workshop paper and prototype, not a broadly deployed standard or independent assurance service.

The reported design trusts the TEE vendor and measured base, omits several production details such as replay prevention and key rotation, and reports material cost overhead relative to ordinary inference.

candidates.title: Making AI-Assisted Grant Evaluation Auditable without Exposing the Model
candidates.relevance: A second, independently authored evaluation-bundle design that explicitly signs and timestamps the input, model, rubric and output measurements, narrowing any defensible Warrantor innovation to a specific interoperable format, completeness model or deployment property.
limitations: The paper is a single-author preprint proposing an architecture rather than reporting an independently reproduced production deployment.

Remote attestation can prove measured execution identity and integrity under assumptions but cannot establish fairness, scientific validity, completeness of real-world evidence or correctness of the evaluation rubric.

candidates.title: ATTESTATION-v1, ACTION-v1 and Reference Verifiers
candidates.relevance: A current implemented receipt family showing that signed AI model-call decisions and agent-action authorization records already have open wire formats, Python and TypeScript verifiers, adversarial vectors and a production-gateway claim. It does not pin the provider's actual compute or an evaluation grader, so it bounds rather than fully supplies Warrantor's evaluation-receipt target.
limitations: The specification and production claims are first-party vendor evidence; the managed Seal gateway is not in the open repository and independent deployment evidence was not found in this review.

A gateway signature proves what the gateway asserted for routed traffic, not that the named provider compute ran, that the action executed as authorized, or that omitted traffic and records do not exist.

candidates.title: Amazon Bedrock AgentCore Pricing
candidates.relevance: A current first-party price sheet for the closest managed enforcement comparator, enabling Warrantor to model authorization, gateway, identity, evaluation and runtime costs separately instead of collapsing unlike workloads into a GPU-hour price.
limitations: This is a mutable vendor price sheet, not independent evidence of customer value, realized cost, reliability or technical efficacy.
AWS pricing depends on region, request mix, model usage, CloudWatch and other services; point-in-time examples must be versioned and recalculated for representative Warrantor workloads.

candidates.title: Microsoft Agent 365 Licensing and Pricing FAQ
candidates.relevance: An official point-in-time licensing benchmark showing that a major suite competitor prices agent governance through user licensing, which challenges Warrantor to segment hosted assurance, enforcement and sovereign deployment rather than copy a generic seat-plus-GPU model.
limitations: Licensing terms and list prices can change and negotiated enterprise prices are not public.
Agent 365 bundles a broad Microsoft estate, so its per-user list price is not a clean willingness-to-pay comparator for Warrantor's narrower evidence and assurance layer.

candidates.title: Cloudflare AI Gateway Pricing
candidates.relevance: A first-party benchmark for a gateway competitor whose core analytics, caching and rate-limiting features are free, reinforcing that Warrantor should monetize verifiable assurance, sovereign operation and support rather than commodity proxy features.
limitations: The page is vendor-authored and its free-versus-premium boundary can change without notice.
Cloudflare's global network economics and cross-subsidized platform do not predict Warrantor's costs, achievable margins or buyer willingness to pay.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence Index Report 2026
authors: Stanford Institute for Human-Centered Artificial Intelligence AI Index Steering Committee
candidates.relevance: The broadest high-authority current synthesis for adoption, investment, cost and governance context; useful for bounding demand narratives while preventing Warrantor from presenting self-reported adoption surveys as a direct market-size model.
limitations: Many corporate-adoption measures are drawn from third-party surveys and are self-reported; the report itself cautions that they are directional rather than comprehensive.

AI-wide investment and adoption cannot be converted directly into an addressable market for authority, evidence or containment without buyer counts, budgets, substitution effects and product-specific willingness-to-pay data.

candidates.title: The Enterprise AI Playbook: Lessons from 51 Successful Developments
candidates.relevance: A current empirical counterweight to failure-rate headlines, organized around 51 deployments that reportedly delivered business value and therefore useful for Warrantor pilot design, buyer qualification and adoption-path hypotheses.
limitations: The successful-case sampling design is appropriate for learning patterns but cannot estimate population success rates or market size.
Case reports and executive interviews can be affected by survivorship, disclosure and selection bias; claimed outcomes require case-level scrutiny before use in sales content.

candidates.title: The GenAI Divide: State of AI in Business 2025
candidates.relevance: A widely cited preliminary enterprise-adoption report whose multi-method design and failure narrative merit direct methodological review before repository claims repeat its figures or use them to justify Warrantor's go-to-market plan.
limitations: The report labels its findings preliminary and combines public initiative review, 52 organization interviews and 153 conference-sourced survey responses without providing a population-representative sampling frame.
The headline that 95 percent obtain zero return is frequently overgeneralized beyond the report's operational definition and evidence; it must not be treated as a universal enterprise base rate.

candidates.title: CNCF Annual Cloud Native Survey: The Infrastructure of AI's Future
candidates.relevance: A method-disclosed survey of 628 respondents that supports Kubernetes and cloud-native integration as a mainstream buyer context while emphasizing organizational transformation, CI/CD and resource optimization over model novelty.
limitations: The sample is drawn from the cloud-native community and therefore likely overstates cloud-native and Kubernetes adoption relative to the full enterprise population.
Survey adoption figures do not establish demand for Warrantor, attainable revenue or the superiority of any authority and evidence architecture.

candidates.title: Shaping the Future of Generative AI
candidates.relevance: A transparent 46-question, multi-geography survey with downloadable data that can inform open-source adoption and infrastructure assumptions while allowing Warrantor to inspect sample composition rather than rely on promotional summaries.
limitations: Respondents were sourced substantially from Linux Foundation and partner communities, creating ecosystem-selection bias toward open source and cloud-native practice.
The study concerns generative AI broadly and predates many 2026 agent-governance products; it is context evidence, not a product-market-size estimate.

candidates.title: The State of Commercial Open Source 2025
candidates.publisher: Linux Foundation Research, Serena, and COSSA
candidates.relevance: The strongest current quantitative source found for Warrantor's open-source commercialization strategy, using 25 years of venture data for more than 800 companies plus repository-community indicators.
limitations: The study adopts a broad definition that includes open weights and companies with only a meaningful open component, so its cohort is not equivalent to OSI-licensed infrastructure projects.

It studies venture-backed survivors and outcomes, not bootstrapped projects, customer willingness to pay or causal effects; community and valuation relationships are primarily correlational and the authors include venture and advocacy stakeholders.

candidates.title: The State of Global Open Source 2025
candidates.relevance: A current global survey for understanding why enterprises that depend on open source still purchase commercial support and governance, directly relevant to Warrantor's packaging, trust signals and partnership strategy.
limitations: The Linux Foundation community sampling frame can overrepresent organizations already engaged with open source.
Reported business value and maturity are self-reported; the study cannot validate Warrantor's prices, margins, capital plan or buyer conversion assumptions.

candidates.title: ROI for Open Source Software Contribution
candidates.relevance: A 567-response, method-disclosed study and quantitative model directly relevant to Warrantor's consume-and-contribute doctrine, partner strategy and choice between maintaining forks and investing upstream.
limitations: Eligibility required respondents to use or contribute to open source and provide organizational budget estimates, which narrows generalizability and introduces recall and self-report error.
The model addresses organizational contribution economics broadly, not the security, governance or monetization trade-offs of this specific project.

candidates.title: IndiaAI Compute Price Calculator and Empaneled AI Services
candidates.relevance: The authoritative current India price and supplier baseline for testing Warrantor's GPU-hour pricing and sovereign deployment economics against publicly procured on-demand and reserved compute rather than a single global list price.
limitations: Prices and available instances are dynamic, rupee-denominated and tied to IndiaAI's procurement and subsidy environment; they require dated snapshots and tax, storage, network, support and utilization adjustments.

candidates.title: End-User Policy for AI Services on the Cloud
candidates.relevance: Defines the actual approval, eligibility and subsidy machinery surrounding India's national compute market, including the Program Monitoring and Evaluation Committee and thresholds for larger requests.
limitations: The policy governs subsidized access to empaneled AI cloud services rather than general Indian enterprise procurement or direct purchase of Warrantor software.
Eligibility and subsidy decisions are program-specific and may change; a local incorporated bidder or empaneled service partner may still be required for some routes.

candidates.title: Digital Transformation Basic Standards V4.0
candidates.relevance: A current English government standard that turns Saudi cloud transformation into auditable agency plans, budgets, adoption measures, periodic reporting and corrective decisions, creating concrete evidence outputs and procurement entry points for sovereign Warrantor deployments.
limitations: The standard applies to Saudi government entities and does not itself create demand for Warrantor or specify an AI-agent evidence format.
Security and military agencies have exceptions, while sector regulators, data-classification rules, local-cloud qualification and procurement law impose additional requirements.

candidates.title: Digital Procurement Policy
authors: United Arab Emirates Ministry of Finance
candidates.publisher: Official Platform of the UAE Government
candidates.relevance: The official English procurement overview for UAE federal entities, useful for mapping supplier, approval, audit, quality and price-competition requirements into Warrantor's GCC go-to-market and partner model.

Defense, security, construction, medicines, some international arrangements and public-private partnerships are excluded, and emirate-level procurement can follow different rules.

candidates.title: Artificial Intelligence Guideline 2024
candidates.relevance: The strongest direct procurement and evidence-format source found for a priority GCC market: it mandates an AI register for QCB-regulated entities and enumerates provider identity, contract, risk, audit, substitution and approval fields.

candidates.relevance: Directly supersedes the need for Warrantor to invent a general cross-harness evaluation-result schema: it defines aggregate and instance-level semantics, provenance, model, framework, generation, judge, dataset, metric and uncertainty fields plus converters and validation.
limitations: The paper is a preprint and its reported repository scale is coalition-reported rather than independently recounted in this wave.

The schema is strongest for text and single-model evaluation, cannot recover metadata absent from source records, does not run evaluations, uses UUID run identity rather than a canonical receipt fingerprint and provides no signer-authenticated artifact profile.

Local reproduction at commit 687b7a36902c01db8a80f0b719d8861d6494f550 passed 997 tests with 45 skips and one terminal-color assertion failure caused by capture-disabled execution; semantic converter and validation paths passed.

candidates.title: Dead Simple Signing Envelope v1.0.2
authors: Secure Systems Lab and DSSE contributors
candidates.relevance: DSSE is the minimal, widely reused authentication envelope Warrantor should consume for JSON and binary predicates: it signs the exact payload bytes together with an authenticated type while avoiding canonicalization dependencies and supporting threshold verification across trusted keys.
limitations: DSSE deliberately leaves key discovery, PKI, exclusive key ownership, algorithms, time, revocation, transparency and trust policy out of scope.

The keyid is an unauthenticated hint and must not drive security decisions, and verification is unsafe if an application reparses an unverified envelope instead of consuming the exact verified payload bytes.
A valid DSSE signature authenticates a statement by an accepted key; it does not prove truthful content, measured execution, policy authority, complete mediation or receipt-set completeness.

candidates.title: RFC 9943: An Architecture for Trustworthy and Transparent Digital Supply Chains
candidates.relevance: The IETF SCITT architecture is the authoritative current transparency and registration layer for signed supply-chain statements and directly informs Warrantor's optional public or consortium evidence publication profile.
limitations: SCITT proves issuer authentication, accepted registration and VDS inclusion; it explicitly permits false statements and selective submission and does not define trusting issuers, statement semantics, complete event capture or enforcement.
Authentication and authorization to a transparency service, key discovery, compromised-key revocation and application-specific liability remain out of scope.
Statement order in the VDS need not equal issuance order, and public or even hash-only transparency can leak sensitive metadata and sequence information.

candidates.title: RFC 9942: CBOR Object Signing and Encryption (COSE) Receipts
candidates.relevance: This Standards Track specification is the normative proof container beneath SCITT receipts and a strong consume target wherever Warrantor needs compact inclusion, consistency or related VDS proofs in COSE ecosystems.
limitations: Proof encodings are VDS-specific and the RFC warns implementers not to expect interoperability across VDSs; migration requires a new security and privacy analysis.
The format proves the property represented by a valid VDS proof, not statement truth, execution, event capture or the completeness of everything that should have been registered.
Receipt validity periods, revocation and suspension status are explicitly out of scope, while log length and header parameters can leak operational information.

candidates.title: RFC 9711: The Entity Attestation Token (EAT)
candidates.relevance: EAT is the current Standards Track claims framework Warrantor should profile for device, process, TEE and confidential-computing evidence rather than inventing a new measured-state token vocabulary.
limitations: EAT is a flexible message-format framework: it defines no message flow, no verifier policy and no minimum security level for an entity, attester or claim implementation.
All COSE/JOSE combinations are allowed, including an Unsecured JWT, unless a Warrantor profile narrows them; a signature alone is therefore not synonymous with a trustworthy measured execution.
Claim trustworthiness depends on implementation, key protection, endorsements, reference values and verifier processing, and identifiers and device-state claims create significant privacy risks.

candidates.title: RFC 9334: Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) Architecture
candidates.relevance: RATS supplies the indispensable role and trust architecture for Warrantor's measured-execution and confidential-computing profiles, especially the separation of raw evidence, verifier appraisal and a relying party's authorization decision.
limitations: RFC 9334 is an Informational architecture, not a wire protocol, claims schema or complete assurance case; specific formats, transports, algorithms and appraisal policies must be profiled elsewhere.

Attestation results are only as strong as the attester, verifier, endorsements, reference values and policies, and freshness can only narrow recentness because state may change immediately after evidence generation.
Evidence and results can expose sensitive device, software, policy and user information, and unprotected evidence transfers responsibility to the trusted conveyance path and verifier.

candidates.title: RFC 9999: RATS Conceptual Message Wrapper
candidates.relevance: CMW is the newest normative interoperability layer for carrying RATS evidence, attestation results, endorsements, reference values and appraisal policies across heterogeneous protocols and formats; it can prevent a Warrantor-specific transport island.
limitations: CMW defines encapsulation, typing and carriage, not a security format or evidence semantics; the producer and hosting protocol remain responsible for integrity, confidentiality, freshness and policy binding.
An unprotected Collection CMW is vulnerable to item manipulation, substitution and misleading composition unless the collection or its members are cryptographically or semantically bound.
Adoption, implementation maturity and interoperability across the large format and transport surface still require independent evaluation.
